items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: FAN (Family, Associates, and Neighbors) plan created after pl_002's direct census and vital-record searches returned only indirect or secondary evidence of parentage. The 1880 census (first to state relationships explicitly), later censuses, Thomas Flynn's marriage record, siblings' post-1906 death certificates, Patrick's obituary, and Thomas's death/burial record are now the primary vehicles for upgrading the conclusion from probable to proved.

The 1880 U.S. census was the first federal enumeration to record each household member's relationship to the head. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) would be approximately 62 years old. Finding Patrick listed as 'son' of Thomas in the 1880 household would directly state the parent-child relationship — upgrading all prior indirect (co-residence only) evidence to direct evidence of parentage. The 1880 census is fully indexed and free on FamilySearch. Search variant spellings: Flyn, Flinn. This is the single highest-probability step toward a proved conclusion.

The 1870 census does not record relationships explicitly, but lists all household members by name. Thomas (~52 in 1870) and Patrick (~25) may appear together; more critically, this census would name Thomas's wife — the candidate mother whose identity remains unknown in this project. Note: re-examining the original 1850 census image already in the project (src_001, ark:/61903/1:1:MXYZ) before executing this search may reveal her name directly, since household members beyond Patrick and Thomas were not extracted. The 1870 household also reveals siblings still at home by name and age, which unlocks pli_011 (sibling death certificates). Variant spellings: Flyn, Flinn.

The 1900 census collects each person's father's birthplace and mother's birthplace. Patrick Flynn (~55 in 1900) in his own household would state his parents' birthplaces on the face of the record. If consistent with Thomas Flynn (born Ireland), this constitutes an additional independent line of evidence from Patrick's own reporting — distinct from the 1850 and 1860 co-residence assertions. Patrick's 1900 neighbors may include siblings or cousins who further define the FAN cluster. Patrick died 1908, making 1900 the last census in which he would appear. Collection is fully indexed and free on FamilySearch.

Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's candidate mother is the family-formation record required by GPS parentage standards — it names both parties and, if the mother's first marriage, yields her maiden name. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) indexes 1.2M records with 607K images for this county. If Thomas married in Pennsylvania before Patrick's ~1845 birth, the marriage falls circa 1840–1848; if he married in Ireland before emigrating, the PA search may be negative and an Irish-records fallback should follow. Per the locality guide, some anthracite-region parish films are browse-only image groups — both indexed search and image browsing may be required. If the mother's surname proves to differ from Thomas's (suggesting a prior marriage), add a separate search for each of her marriage records and a sibling's record naming her parents, rather than relying on this one record for her maiden name.

Any sibling of Patrick who died after 1906 (when Pennsylvania civil registration began) would have a death certificate naming both parents. Execute this item after pli_008 (1870 census) and pli_007 (1880 census) have established the siblings' names. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968' (collection 2255317) holds 4.2M records. Sibling death certificates provide the same evidence type as Patrick's own 1908 certificate (a_013) but from independent informants — if multiple siblings' certificates all name Thomas Flynn as father, the convergence substantially strengthens the conclusion. Date range is governed by siblings' plausible lifespans: Thomas b. ~1818 could have fathered children into the 1860s, who could survive into the 1930s or later — the window is not capped at Patrick's own death in 1908.

Patrick Flynn died in 1908 in Schuylkill County. The anthracite coal region had active newspapers — notably the Miners' Journal (Pottsville) and the Mahanoy City Daily American — that regularly published obituaries naming surviving family members, birth origins, and sometimes parents. A 1908 obituary for Patrick naming Thomas Flynn as his father, or naming surviving siblings (whose identity will be known from pli_007–pli_008), would add an independent documentary line corroborating the parentage claim. Search Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free, covers Pennsylvania papers through 1963) first; then Newspapers.com (subscription, broader coverage) if Chronicling America returns nothing for Schuylkill County in 1908.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, ~32 in 1850) likely died between 1870 and 1910. His death or burial record — a Pennsylvania state death certificate if post-1906 (collection 2255317), a Catholic parish burial register entry, or a cemetery record — would name surviving family members and possibly list children. A newspaper death notice for Thomas would likely name Patrick as a surviving son. Finding Thomas's burial parish also identifies the family's home church, enabling a more targeted search under pli_010 (marriage register). The prior probate search (log_006) returned negative; this item targets the death and burial record separately. Date range is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan (~1818 birth), not by Patrick's research window. Variant spellings: Flyn, Flinn.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

# Locality Guide — Muhlenberg County, Kentucky (1840–1920)

## Jurisdiction

**Muhlenberg County** was formed in **1798** from Christian and Logan counties. No further internal boundary changes affected its territory. The county seat is Greenville. All local records (court, probate, marriages) are held at the county level; post-1911 vital records are held at the state level.

---

## ⚠ Critical Finding — Death Certificates

**Statewide death certificates begin 1 January 1911.** No state certificate exists for any death before that date ([Kentucky Online Genealogy Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Online_Genealogy_Records)).

Elijah Wilkins (b. c. 1814) would have been ~97 years old in 1911. A death before 1911 is far more probable. **The question's premise — "using Kentucky death certificates" — can only be satisfied if he survived to age 97+.** If he died earlier, no certificate will be found, and the death must be bracketed through probate, census, and burial records.

---

## Available Records

### 1. Death / Vital Records

| Source | Coverage | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch col. 1417491 — *Kentucky Deaths, 1911–1967* | 1911–1967 | Indexed + images (2.9M records) | Statewide certificates; nothing before 1 Jan 1911 |
